title: Decoding Compound Flood Risk Under Nonstationary Conditions: A Separable Parametric Framework Revealing the Heterogeneous Effects of Driving Mechanisms
content:
Abstract

Compound flooding in coastal environments arises from the interaction of extreme precipitation and elevated coastal water levels. Existing approaches typically rely either on process-based hydrodynamic simulations or statistical characterizations of hazard drivers, constraining the capacity to quantify the contribution of individual mechanisms to inundation and the propagation of evolving hazard regimes into flood risk. This study develops a holistic compound flood risk framework, comprising an optimal estimator for predicting inundation levels under interacting hydrological stressors (i.e., rainfall intensity, storm surge, and antecedent streamflow), and a probabilistic model for the estimation of flood exceedance rates conditional on the driving mechanisms. A case study over the Greater Boston area demonstrates accurate reproduction of inundation patterns across a diverse set of historical storms, with low errors. Analyses conducted over sequential temporal segments reveal localized hotspots of flood risk intensification that may be misestimated by long-term aggregation. Results further highlight that changes in rainfall intensity and frequency do not translate uniformly into flood risk but, instead, drive spatially heterogeneous responses. In upstream regions, rainfall trends control flood risk changes, whereas coastal processes modulate intensification patterns near the estuarine boundary. By coupling hydrodynamic simulations with a statistically rigorous modeling scheme, the framework facilitates the isolation and quantification of the relative contributions of interacting flood drivers to climate-induced shifts in flood risk, in a computationally efficient and interpretable manner. These insights can inform resilience planning, targeted mitigation strategies, and climate adaptation efforts in coastal and estuarine environments.
